newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: VIENNA PROSECUTOR EXAMINES BELGIUM BRIBERY CHARGE.
newsitem.headline: VIENNA PROSECUTOR EXAMINES BELGIUM BRIBERY CHARGE.

text.p: Vienna's state prosecutor said on Thursday he was investigating allegations that a subsidiary of listed industrial group Radex-Heraklith (RHI) paid millions of dollars in kickbacks to customers in the 1980s.
Erich Mueller, commercial state prosecutor, told Reuters the inquiry involved the Austrian firm Veitscher Magnesit AG, which was absorbed into RHI in the early 1990s.
"The alleged bribes were paid all over the world. The investigation is concentrating on Italy, Belgium and Portugal, where the legal culture is the same," Mueller said.
In other countries, including parts of the Middle East, kickbacks were legal, making a prosecution in some instances impossible, the state prosecutor added.
Veitscher, which became Veitsch-Radex after its acquisition by RHI, produced refractories to insulate against searing temperatures in the steel, glass and cement industries.

A spokesman for RHI, a world leader in the manufacture of fireproof materials, told Reuters the company's lawyers were drawing up a detailed response to the allegations, which appeared in Thursday's edition of current affairs weekly News.
"But it is is extremely complicated, given that we are looking back 10 years and some people are now retired," spokesman Peter Hofmann said.
According to News, Veitscher paid around 500 million schillings ($40 million) in bribes to business partners -- mostly buyers for the steel industry -- during the 1980s.
Hofmann noted Veitscher Magnesit no longer existed.
"And Veitsch-Radex was not involved. (The alleged incidents) do not reflect the style of Veitsch-Radex," he said.
"Veitsch-Radex has achieved its high world ranking through its technical innovation and the quality of its products."
The state prosecutor said he was examining documents, purportedly written by Veitscher management, that showed bribes were sometimes disguised as expenses.
On other occasions customers were over-charged and the extra cash returned as a kick-back.
According to News, the second method was most common in Italy, Belgium, the Far East and Argentina. The magazine claimed much of the money passed through a Swiss bank account.
Hofmann categorically denied a second set of allegations, also made in News, that RHI had been involved in price fixing.
"Worldwide our industry is so fragmented that it would be impossible to form a cartel," he said.
RHI shares, which are listed in Vienna's blue-chip ATX index, were 3.5 schillings down at 568.5 in a generally buoyant market.
